newsitem.title: GERMANY: Compaq sees German rebound, future growth.
newsitem.headline: Compaq sees German rebound, future growth.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. said on Thursday it expected a rebound in German sales powered by new low-cost personal computers as part of a forecast 25 percent annual growth over the next four years.

The new machines, due in the next few months and priced below 3,000 marks ($1,780), would enable Compaq to respond to fierce price competition that eroded its market German share by two points to 7.8 percent in 1996, CEO Eckhard Pfeiffer said.

Compaq was also broadening its product line this year into handheld PCs and networking products and later planned to add new PC-based entertainment systems, Internet products and computer services as it aimed to more than double sales to $40 billion by the end of the decade, Pfeiffer said.
"It shouldn't be a surprise if we grow 25 percent a year for the next four years," Pfeiffer told a news conference. "We averaged 50 percent growth in the last four years."
In 1996, Compaq's worldwide sales rose 23 percent to $18.1 billion, while European sales increased 12 percent to $6 billion.

In Germany, sales rose 7.6 percent to 1.4 billion marks, although unit shipments stagnated, European chief Andreas Barth told Reuters. Compaq was hurt because it had few low-priced desktop and portable models for most of the year, he said.
German unit Compaq Computer GmbH shipped just over 300,000 PCs in 1996, the company said, quoting market researcher Dataquest.

Its share of home PC sales fell to 3.5 percent, from 7.5 percent in 1995. In sales to businesses, it share slipped to 12.9 percent from 13.3 percent, and in portable PCs its share dropped to 14.7 percent from 16 percent, the company said.
Its only increase came in the server segment, where its share rose to 25.6 percent from 24.7 percent.
Along with adding low-priced PCs, Compaq plans to increase focus on small and mid-sized German companies, that have not installed PCs as rapidly as large corporations.
"This will give us another segment to play in," said Kurt Dobitsch, head of Compaq's German unit. "This segment will clearly become larger this year."

For the future, Compaq was counting on the explosion in use of the Internet to drive worldwide sales to between $20 billion and $25 billion in 1997 and to between $25 billion and $30 billion in 1998, Pfeiffer said.
The company expected sales to climb to between $30 billion and $35 billion in 1999 and to reach $40 billion in 2000, he said.

"The Internet has driven an incredible level of activity," he said in an interview. "I personally believe the underlying strength (of the Internet-driven boom) is that the growth is self-perpetuating."
Taking advantage of the Internet "is something that all companies are trying to accomplish -- being more efficient. In four years Internet commerce will be huge," he said.

Compaq would log into Internet growth by expanding its lines of modems and networking switches called hubs and routers. At the same time, its handheld PC Companion would break into another high-growth market, Pfeiffer said.
"This is not an experiment," he said, shaking off any comparison with Apple Computer Inc.'s famed Newton handheld flop. "It is a product category we always talked about."
Compaq would ship tens of thousands of PC Companions this year and had underestimated demand since its introduction in the United States. European versions are due around mid-1997.

But some analysts were sceptical about its chances in Europe where digital cellular phones can transmit data from mobile computers. "If you have a (digital) phone, who needs one of those things?" said Dataquest's Chris Jones in London.

In coming years, Compaq expected to expand its line of computer and educational products for small children and branch into new markets with products that combine computer, television and Internet technology, Pfeiffer said.
($ = 1.684 German Marks)
